body_markdown:
At least 34 children in Bihar, India, were taken to hospital after allegedly consuming food contaminated with laundry detergent during a school lunch. Officials have ordered an inquiry.


## Bihar School Lunch Incident Leaves Dozens of Children Ill


At least 34 children were taken to hospital in Bihar, India, after reportedly falling ill following a school lunch that was allegedly contaminated with laundry detergent. The incident occurred at a government-run school in Nalanda district, raising fresh concerns about food safety and the supervision of India's large school meal programme.


According to reports, students at Parsa Middle School were served boiled rice along with a potato and soya vegetable curry on Tuesday. Several children reportedly complained of a burning sensation in their stomachs after eating the meal. Some also experienced vomiting, dizziness and other symptoms, prompting school authorities to arrange medical treatment.


The children were subsequently taken to a nearby hospital after their condition did not immediately improve. Local health officials later said the students were in stable condition.


## How Did Laundry Detergent End Up in the School Meal?


The school headteacher, Shailendra Kumar Singh, alleged that laundry detergent powder was mistakenly given to students who had asked for additional salt with their lunch.


According to the account reported by The Independent, one of three cooks working in the school kitchen was serving food when some children requested salt. The headteacher claimed that detergent powder was accidentally served instead.


The school meal was reportedly supplied through a non-governmental organisation, meaning questions may also arise about how ingredients and food preparation materials were stored and handled.


Authorities will need to establish precisely how the alleged mix-up occurred. This includes determining whether detergent and food ingredients were stored close together, whether containers were clearly labelled and whether adequate kitchen supervision was in place.


At this stage, the reported explanation remains an allegation and should not be treated as a confirmed finding until the official investigation is completed.


## Children Taken to Hospital After Developing Symptoms


Students reportedly began experiencing symptoms soon after consuming the meal. Some children complained of stomach burning, while others reportedly experienced dizziness and vomiting.


School staff provided first aid before the affected pupils were taken to hospital. Nalanda civil surgeon Jai Prakash Singh described the situation as food poisoning and said the children's health conditions were stable.


The response from medical authorities will be closely watched as officials determine whether the symptoms were caused by detergent contamination or another issue involving the food.


Although the children were reported to be stable, the incident has highlighted the importance of immediate medical assessment whenever students show signs of possible poisoning or food contamination.


## Government Orders Investigation


Bihar minister Shravan Kumar visited the affected children at the hospital and said a detailed inquiry would be carried out.


The investigation is expected to examine how the school meal was prepared, how ingredients and other substances were stored, and whether established safety procedures were followed.


Food safety investigations are particularly important in schools because meals are prepared and distributed to large numbers of children. Even a single mistake in the kitchen can potentially affect many students.


The incident also raises broader questions about the responsibilities of schools, meal providers, kitchen staff and local authorities in ensuring that children receive safe food.


## Why India's Midday Meal Scheme Matters


The incident has occurred within one of the world's largest school feeding programmes. India's government-supported midday meal initiative provides cooked meals to children in government and government-aided schools.


The programme is intended to improve children's nutrition while also encouraging school attendance and reducing dropout rates. For many families, the school meal can be an important source of daily nutrition.


The scale of the programme makes food safety particularly significant. Meals are prepared and distributed across a huge network of schools, meaning effective training, monitoring, hygiene standards and supply-chain controls are essential.


Any contamination incident can therefore have consequences beyond the immediate health effects. It can also undermine parents' confidence in a programme designed to support children's wellbeing and education.


## Previous School Food Safety Concerns


The Bihar incident is not an isolated example of concerns surrounding school meals in India.


The Independent reported that more than 20 students in Telangana fell ill in January after eating contaminated school food. There have also been previous reports involving suspected contamination of school lunches in different parts of the country.


In 2025, India's National Human Rights Commission launched an inquiry after reports that more than 100 children became ill following a school lunch that was allegedly contaminated by a dead snake. Hundreds of children had reportedly consumed the meal at a school in Bihar.


These incidents underline the need for strong food safety controls throughout the preparation and distribution process.


## What Could Prevent Similar Incidents?


Preventing accidental contamination requires more than simply investigating individual incidents after they happen. Schools and meal providers need clear procedures covering every stage of food preparation.


Kitchen workers should receive appropriate food safety training, while ingredients and non-food substances should be stored separately. Containers should be clearly labelled, and potentially hazardous cleaning products should never be kept where they could be confused with food ingredients.


Regular inspections can also help identify unsafe practices before they result in illness. Schools may benefit from written procedures for receiving ingredients, preparing meals, storing cleaning products and responding to suspected contamination.


Most importantly, staff should have clear instructions about what to do when children report unusual tastes, smells or physical symptoms after eating.


## What Happens Next?


The investigation in Nalanda will be important in determining exactly what happened at Parsa Middle School. Officials will need to establish whether detergent was mistakenly served, how it entered the food service area and whether any procedural failures contributed to the incident.


The immediate priority remains the health of the affected children. Authorities have said their condition is stable, but continued medical observation may be necessary depending on the symptoms experienced.


The case also provides a reminder that food safety is particularly important in schools, where one kitchen can serve meals to dozens or hundreds of children.


For parents and communities, the outcome of the inquiry will likely be closely watched. A transparent investigation and appropriate corrective measures could help prevent a similar incident from happening again.
